DEFINITION: If thunder sound is within 30 seconds of lightning flash, seek shelter.
The steepest slope a vehicle can climb without the front bumper scraping the ground.
When the vehicle’s underside is stuck on the ground, making it hard to move.
The biggest hump a vehicle can drive over without scraping its belly.
A V-shaped two-leg connection that shares the pull between two attachment points.
Emergency escape from ground electricity by hopping away with both feet together.
Friction increases as a rope bends around a surface, making the rope harder to pull.
See Disabled Vehicle.
Block placed against a tire to stop a vehicle from rolling.
A hook with a U-shaped pin-end that connects to chain or rigging hardware.
Control that lets the winch pull with motor power or unwind freely by hand.
See Solenoid.
The winch’s electrical box. It holds the contactor or solenoids, control electronics, and wireless receiver (for the remote).
The center part of a rope that supports the strands and helps the rope keep its shape.
A D-shaped metal ring fixed to a vehicle as a recovery attachment point.
A weighted blanket placed on a tensioned line to reduce whip if the line breaks.
The danger zone formed where tensioned winch lines make a triangle.
A strong object buried in the ground to act as an anchor when no tree, rock, or vehicle is available.
The steepest slope a vehicle can leave without the rear bumper scraping the ground.
When lightning hits a person, vehicle, tree, or object directly.
The vehicle that is stuck or disabled, and is being recovered.
Two shortening line legs sharing the load to create 2:1 MA.
One level of rope wrapped around the winch drum.
How long a machine can work before it needs a rest to prevent overheating.
The attachment in front of the winch that guides the line smoothly onto the drum.
A tiny thread of synthetic material used to build synthetic rope.
Extra safety allowance for real-world uncertainty.
The seconds between seeing the lightning flash and hearing thunder, used to estimate how far away the storm is.
How deep can the vehicle be submerged in water, for a limited period of time
Winch mode that lets the operator pull out line by hand without using the motor.
The steepness of a slope.
Space between the lowest vehicle part and the ground.
Electricity spreading through the ground after lightning strikes or a live power line touches down.
Gross Vehicle Weight; what the vehicle weighs right now with everything in it.
A metal U-shaped connector with a pin, used to connect recovery gear.
A smooth rope guide with a polished opening, used with synthetic rope.
Curved metal connector used to attach a line, chain, or strap.
A short strap used to pull the hook while keeping hands clear.
A FEMA form that shows the recovery plan and who is in charge.
A FEMA log to document what happens during the recovery operation.
A FEMA gear list showing what is available and ready to use.
A field-made anchor when no fixed or vehicle anchor is available.
Person who leads the recovery and leads decision making.
The area no one should stand in because it can be deadly.
Using a stretchy rope or strap to pull a stuck vehicle free.
The direction the rope strands twist together.
Pulling force carried by the winch line.
How fast the winch line moves in or out.
The route pulling force takes through the winch line, hardware, anchor, and vehicle.
Mechanical Advantage; a setup that lets you pull more weight with less effort.
Minimum Breaking Strength; the lowest force that made the gear break during testing.
Required rope wraps left on the drum to keep the line safely secured to the winch.
Soft mud or ground that traps the tires of a vehicle.
See Shortening Leg.
A winch line with one or more legs that get shorter during the pull.
The pull power a rig should have before friction weakens it.
Pulling from the side so the winch or operator can stay in a safer position.
A decision cycle for stressful situations: observe what is happening, orient to why it matters, decide what to do, act, then observe again.
Personal Protective Equipment; safety gear the operator wears to protect their body. Each operator must have their own.
The angle of winch line relative to ground.
Safe pulling spot on a vehicle.
A smooth ring that redirects the winch line; it is not a pulley.
Rigging that changes the force’s direction without any mechanical advantage.
Hand control that lets the operator run the winch from a safer distance.
Short code that describes the rig type, geometry, anchor, and mode of recovery.
Required Line Pull; how much pull is needed to move the disabled vehicle.
Fairlead with rotating rollers, used with wire rope.
The force needed to keep a vehicle rolling in neutral.
The complete line used for pulling, made from strands around a core.
Area outside the danger area where people may stand.
Safety ration between the WLL and the MBS. Higher safety factor means more margin of safety.
The wheel inside a pulley or snatch block that the rope runs over.
A sudden force spike on the rig. It could be from slack, impact, or jerking.
A rope section that moves and gets shorter during the pull.
Lightning jumping from a tree, vehicle, or object to a nearby person.
A sideways pull on gear that should only be pulled straight.
Only one shortening leg of the rope in the pull.
One person or unit assigned to one specific task.
See Terrain multipliers
When a tight rope or strap suddenly flies back after breaking or coming loose.
A side-opening pulley used to redirect line or add mechanical advantage.
A strong synthetic-rope loop used to connect recovery gear instead of a metal shackle.
The winch’s main power switch. It sends battery power to the motor and controls forward or reverse.
A compound pulley setup that gives mechanical advantage. “Burton” is an old naval word for a small pulley system.
Person who watches the operator’s blind spots and guides vehicle movement.
A fixed object used as an anchor. It should not move.
A rope section that does not get shorter during the pull.
A winch line that stays the same length during the pull.
A main bundle inside a rope. In steel rope, it is made of wires. In synthetic rope, it is made of fibers or yarns.
Extra holding force from mire.
Winch line made from strong fiber.
Number that accounts for harder pulling on soft ground.
Metal insert inside a rope loop that protects it from wear.
Ball used for towing a trailer; never use it for recovery pulling.
Vehicle pulling spot made for towing; this is NOT a recovery point and should not be used for recovery.
A low-stretch strap for slow, steady pulls; not a kinetic rope.
Grip between the tires and the ground.
A wide strap wrapped around a tree to protect the bark and create an anchor.
Electricity reaching upward from the ground toward lightning.
A secured vehicle used as an anchor. It should not move.
See Snapback.
Winch part that holds the load when the motor stops.
A single metal thread used to build a steel-rope strand.
Winch line made from steel wires twisted into strands.
Working Load Limit; the maximum load gear is rated to carry in normal use. Above this, gear can be permanently damaged.
